title: Pacing and leading in a speech
header_line: Jose's analysis of a book we are still naming. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: How does a good speaker get you to say yes before the point?

Jose said that he listens to as many public speeches as he can to learn, whatever his or anyone's political views. He said the technique is called pacing and leading: when you pace, you get people moving with what you say, then you lead.
A student said that she opened by setting up the night by saying big things, so you feel something big is coming.

Jose said that if you start with once upon a time there lived a little boy, you take people to a magical world, an emotional one. He said that the speaker also grounded the feeling by saying we are all feeling it here, as if you were already feeling it.
Jose said: let the words jump out at you. If I meet you, I am going to listen to your words, and they are going to say something about your personal brand.
He said the speaker paced and paced, and then pivoted to a different word that brought you in: the word fear, and not being steady enough to stand before you, which attaches you to her personally.
A student said that an ambiguous phrase such as more than they needed could mean many things, and Jose asked: who is the judge of who needs more and who needs less?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write a thing you say that people always agree with.
Write what you lead them to next.
Write the opening scene of your next talk.
Write one ambiguous phrase you use and make it exact.
Write the one word that will pivot your talk.

check.q: What did Jose say once upon a time does?
choices: Takes people to an emotional world

check.q: What did Jose say to do with a speaker's words?
choices: Let the words jump out at you

recap: Pace, then lead. Choose the words that set the scene.
